headline: Fiona the hippo died. The hat never came out.
summary: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo hippo born six weeks early in 2017, died Thursday. Eleven days ago a visitor tossed a knit hat in the air, a ceiling fan flung it into her enclosure, and she swallowed it. Vets sedated her twice and ran a 9-foot scope. They borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm. Surgery isn't an option on a grown hippo.

cover_question.q: Why did she eat a hat?

cover_answer: It flew into her enclosure, and she swallowed it.
table_question: If you cause harm by accident, do you still owe something?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Fiona the hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo died on Thursday. A knit hat flew into her home, she swallowed it, and it got stuck inside her, the way a washcloth clogs a bathtub drain. Her doctors stayed with her for eleven days and tried everything they knew. Lots of people loved her, and it's okay to be sad.
5-7.why: A stuck hat is something they can picture. Say she died, and let them be sad.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid thing for the whole story, so the script gives them the hat, stuck like a washcloth in a drain. Cantor found this age reads your face before your words, so say 'died' plainly and let the sadness show. Expect 'can they get another Fiona?' No. There are two other hippos. Neither is her.

8-12.script: A visitor at the Cincinnati Zoo tossed a knit hat in the air. A ceiling fan shot it through a gap, and Fiona swallowed it. A hippo's stomach has several chambers, like a cow's, so the hat hid where a scope couldn't find it. Vets can't cut a grown hippo open, so they waited for it to pass.
8-12.why: A chain with no villain: a toss, a fan, a gap, a stomach that hides.
8-12.why_long: At nine a child wants the chain and wants to know whose fault it was. The script hands them the chain and no villain: a toss, a fan, a gap, a stomach built in chambers that hid the hat from a scope. The mechanism beats a verdict. Expect 'why don't they ban hats?' The zoo calls it an accident it couldn't repeat if it tried.

13-17.script: Specialists said surgery wasn't an option: skin two inches thick, and days out of water to heal. So the vets waited for her to pass the hat. Was that the right call, or the only one? Second: zoos have warned for years about objects tossed into habitats. Does one small gap above a window count as negligence?
13-17.why: The vets did every step on the list, and she still died. Hold both.
13-17.why_long: A seventeen-year-old can hold a sad outcome and a defensible process at once: every step the vets describe, and a hippo that died anyway. Kuhn says arguing well is practised, so the script asks whether waiting was a choice or the only option. Expect 'would surgery have saved her?' Nobody knows. The specialists said no.

5-7.q: Why did she eat a hat?
5-7.a: It landed in her enclosure and she swallowed it. Nobody meant for that to happen, and her doctors tried for eleven days to get it out.

8-12.q: Why didn't they just cut it out?
8-12.a: Skin two inches thick, and days out of water to heal. Specialists said no.
Nobody's, the zoo says. A fan flung the hat through a gap.

13-17.q: Could they have found it sooner?
13-17.a: Two sedations, an ultrasound and a 9-foot scope found nothing.
The zoo says it was an accident. Nobody in the articles blames them.
